title: The world is waking up to the Montney’s vast natural gas reserves. Will Canada seize the opportunity?
html:
Just west of Grande Prairie, Alta., past the truck dealerships on Highway 43 and into the endless flat farmland, there is a sea of natural gas most countries would die for.

The Montney Formation stretches 130,000 square kilometres, straddling Alberta’s border with British Columbia, and it is brimming with hundreds of trillions of cubic feet of gas. The volume alone is staggering, and the region’s potential is almost unmatched.

Around the world, quality gas fields have been producing for years – sometimes decades – but the Montney is just getting started. Only 6 per cent of its gas has been unearthed, and the cost to produce it just keeps falling as technology advances.

Yet, until very recently, no one seemed to care.

The Montney’s prospects have been talked about for two decades, ever since Calgary’s Arc Resources Ltd. tried a new production technique, known as horizontal drilling and multistage fracking, to release natural gas trapped in the formation’s tight rock. But the region quickly lost its lustre. Just as it was getting going, American producers deployed the same practices in places such as Pennsylvania, and they, too, hit the jackpot.

For Canadian gas producers, it was a sea change. The U.S. used to be Canada’s top export market. In a flash, it became Canada’s top competitor. The new rivalry, coupled with a global commodity rout, was brutal for Montney producers, including Arc and Encana Corp.

The outlook has been improving the past few years, particularly since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and upended the global gas market. After nearly a decade of pain, the Montney finally started seeing some acquisitions of assets and companies.

But it wasn’t until April when the world really started paying attention. Out of nowhere, Shell PLC SHEL-N swooped in and paid $19-billion for Arc, accelerating a new rush into the Montney. The global energy giant is constantly weighing investment opportunities around the world, and even with all these options, it still chose Canada.

“The Montney is just such a prolific gas resource,” Stastia West, the company’s country head, said in an interview. The region, she added, is as good as marketed – its gas is both abundant and low-cost.

Of course, Shell can be seen as talking up its own book. The company is the lead backer of LNG Canada, the expansive liquefied-natural-gas export facility on Canada’s West Coast, and it needs more gas to feed the plant.

But Canada’s LNG potential has also hit an inflection point. A decade ago, Canada had more than 20 potential export facilities on the table, but almost all of them petered out – victims of either environmental concerns, pushback from Indigenous communities or falling natural gas prices. Sometimes, all three.

How things have changed. Prime Minister Mark Carney has re-emphasized natural resource development to bolster Canada’s economy during the trade war with the U.S., and B.C. just elected a new Premier who campaigned on tripling LNG production by 2035.

In September, Shell and its partners greenlit Phase 2 of LNG Canada, doubling the plant’s export capacity, and now, other global backers are dusting off their old West Coast LNG plans. After Iran shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in March, trapping roughly 20 per cent of the world’s LNG exports, Canadian gas suddenly looked much more appealing, particularly to Asian countries who had already been big buyers.

There are also new sources of demand. Ottawa is keen on building domestic data centres to secure AI data sovereignty, and the Alberta government has opened its arms to those developers. These facilities will need new power plants, and the feedstock will include Montney natural gas.

At the same time, the proposed Pacific Link pipeline could ship one million more barrels of Canadian oil per day, and producers need condensate to help move their thick sludge through the pipe. Condensate is a byproduct of natural gas production in the region.

Canadian Natural Resources is one of the major landholders and natural gas producers operating in Western Canada. Its Knopcik processing facility is located near Grande Prairie, Alta., in the Montney.Jesse Boily/The Globe and Mail

It’s all ignited a flurry of acquisitions. After Shell’s big purchase, Ovintiv Inc., formerly Encana, paid $890-million for Logan Energy Corp. in October, and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. just paid $2.5-billion, including debt, for Advantage Energy Ltd.

Investors, though, are still unsure of what to think. The local natural gas price in the region, known as the AECO price, is trading at rock-bottom levels. There just isn’t enough local demand to absorb the endless supply. And it could stay that way for years, because the Montney’s promise will take time to materialize.

Yet, the potential is also undeniable, and it supports Ottawa’s thesis. Mr. Carney tells anyone who will listen that Canada has what the world wants, and when it comes to the Montney, it’s absolutely true.

To understand why investors are still timid about Canada’s natural gas prospects, consider Ovintiv OVV-T.

In 2008, when the Canadian energy icon was called Encana, it proposed splitting in two to capitalize on a belief that natural gas was the fuel of the future. With AECO gas trading near US$13 per million British thermal units, or MMBtus, management hived off the company’s oil sands assets, creating what is now Cenovus Energy Inc., and kept its gas portfolio.

It was a disaster. Four years later, the shock of newfound U.S. shale gas sent the AECO price tumbling to US$2, and Encana, once Canada’s most valuable company, nearly collapsed. To save itself, the company focused on U.S. oil under an American chief executive, moved its headquarters to Denver and changed its name.

Two decades later, Ovintiv, of all companies, is betting on the Montney again.

The company’s current CEO, Brendan McCracken, a Canadian, not only bought Logan Energy this fall, but he also signed three other Montney acquisitions in the past few years, including buying NuVista Energy Ltd. for $3.5-billion and acquiring assets from Paramount Resources Ltd. and Advantage Energy.

What’s so appealing now?

To start, the Montney is still a massive, undeveloped region. It spreads from south of Grande Prairie, Alta., to north of Fort St. John in northeastern British Columbia. Gas companies refer to this as the areal extent.

“You can drill thousands and thousands of wells here,” said Chris Carlsen, the CEO of Birchcliff Energy Ltd. BIR-T, one of the first companies to drill in the Montney, in 2007. And because producers have learned how to get more gas out of each well, the Montney has been aging like wine. Thanks to technological advances, he said, “this one’s getting better.”

Chris Carlsen, president and CEO of Birchcliff Energy. The company was one of the first to drill in the Montney nearly two decades ago.Amir Salehi/The Globe and Mail

Then there’s the thickness. The Montney siltstones that contain gas, formed during the Triassic Period, are often found 2,000 to 3,000 metres below the surface and the tight rock ranges from 30 to 300 metres thick.

It used to be that a company would drop a single pipe straight down and produce whatever came back up. Eventually, gas producers started drilling into harder rock and shooting a mixture of sand, water and chemicals to fracture it and let the gas escape through the cracks. The pipes would also turn horizontal, so they not only went deep, but could also spread two to three miles wide. This is the technique that Arc experimented with two decades ago.

Because the Montney is so thick, producers can repeat this at different depths from the same well pad. Each well pad might have eight or 12 well heads, and their pipes shoot down and out in all different directions. Under the surface, it looks like a spider web.

The Montney is also rich with natural gas liquids, which is what Ovintiv finds so enticing. With each of his successive acquisitions, Mr. McCracken stressed that the assets being purchased are rich with condensate, which changes the profit margin on each well. Dry natural gas doesn’t fetch much at AECO prices, but Mr. McCracken argued condensate is the best natural resource in Canada because it’s “the only one that attracts a global premium price.” Even Canadian oil trades at a discount.

Ironically, depressed local gas prices have also made the Montney more appealing. For quite some time, the Permian Basin that stretches from West Texas into New Mexico has been talked about as the hottest energy play in North America – and for good reason. The oil there is easy to produce and it is abundant.

Yet, the Permian has become expensive, with assets recently trading hands for about US$7-million per location (effectively, the cost per well). For comparison, recent deals in the Montney have been done at US$1.5-million per location. That’s roughly 80-per-cent cheaper, for arguably the same quality of resource.

Even though the Permian has much more oil than gas, the energy industry harmonizes oil and gas production using a metric known as barrels of oil equivalent, or BOE, and cost per location works the same way.

For recent Montney acquirers, such as Shell, the region’s potential at these prices makes it seem like a steal.

Not only can Shell feed its LNG export expansion with Arc’s gas, it can capitalize on soaring global LNG prices. The second that Canadian gas hits open water, its price jumps from around US$1.50 per MMBtu to around US$25, because the Asian countries who import it are paying a premium now that LNG from the Middle East can’t be shipped.

Ms. West, Shell’s head of Canada, said Asian countries have “huge demand for gas as they work through their own energy transition and look to displace coal.”

As for data centres, the potential is more than just the volume of new power plants being pitched in Alberta. On top of new legislation that requires these facilities to have their own power sources so that they don’t strain the existing grid, their developers also have to factor in backup power.

“We’re talking to these guys,” said Mr. Carlsen. “Not only do they want our gas, they want backup gas from our second plant.” And then, on top of that, they want to build close to natural gas pipelines operated by TC Energy Corp., which dominates Western Canadian gas transmission. The goal, he’s been told, is up to three sources of gas redundancy.

This very scenario is what Mike Rose has been betting on for decades.

The CEO of Tourmaline Oil Corp. TOU-T started drilling in the Montney around the same time as Arc, and Tourmaline is now Canada’s leading gas producer. Sitting in a boardroom in the company’s downtown Calgary office, down the hall from his exotic mineral collection – Mr. Rose is a geologist by training – he’s asked how the Montney stacks up to the almighty Permian.

“Better,” he says.

“Better?”

“Yup.”

The Permian has lots of oil, Mr. Rose acknowledges, “but it’s getting depleted at a pretty good clip.” The Montney, meanwhile, has as much as 645 trillion cubic feet of marketable gas, according to a 2013 report from the Canada Energy Regulator, and only about 40 tcf has been produced. As a baseball fanatic, he put it this way: In the Montney, “you’re top of the first inning.”

He also makes the case that natural gas is a friendlier fuel for the environment. Some of the Asian countries importing Canadian LNG still rely on coal power, and natural gas helps to displace that.

Mr. Rose is biased, of course. There are scores of environmentalists who point out that methane emitted during natural gas production is a potent greenhouse gas that traps heat and contributes to climate change. Wildfires have been raging, and their smoke blanketed large swaths of Canada again last summer.

Plus, China has boosted its own natural gas production, using techniques such as fracking. It’s now the world’s fourth-largest natural gas producer behind the United States, Russia and Iran. China also shocked the world this spring when it displayed resiliency after the Strait of Hormuz closed. The expectation was that China would become desperate for other sources of LNG imports. The reality: It had quietly stockpiled loads of natural gas in tanks, a process that is normally quite difficult to do.

In Canada, meanwhile, the age-old demand and supply principles persist. For all the potential, Montney producers are largely still at the whim of AECO prices, which are depressed. It helps explain why Tourmaline shares are still trading at the same level they did in early 2022.
